div.head: Ps Cn for 32
div.ab: Uelteres uero quos langeran appellant, quia manifeste constat in iis nihil esse periculi, cuilibet licebit sine genuscissione eos custodire. Idem de canibus quos rainehound uocant.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 626 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)
div.ab: But velters (small hunting dogs), which they call langeran, since it is manifestly established that there is no danger in them, anyone shall be permitted to keep without knee-cutting. The same of the dogs which they call rainehound.

note.seg: 'Langohr' hielt für möglich Zupitza; doch ist wahrscheinlich die Form lanlegeran, o. S. 367*, richtiger und das Wort dem Nord. langleggr (Langbein) entlehnt. Vgl. o. S. 534u ueltrarii

Zupitza thought 'Langohr' (long-ear) possible; but the form lanlegeran, above p. 367*, is probably more correct, and the word borrowed from Norse langleggr (long-leg). Cf. above p. 534 note u, ueltrarii

vgl. ebd. Das Compositum fehlt sonst, auch Nordisch. Das erste Glied bedeutet 'Rennthier'. Da Altengl. das Wort (h)rân, Nordisch aber raine (rayne) lautet, so liegt vermuthlich ein Lehnwort vor, wiederum zur Bezeichnung einer besonderen Rasse von Hunden. Rennthierknochen in Caithness und Sutherland kennt Bugge Helge Digtare in .. Edda; MAURER, der Engl. Stud. 1895, S. 61 Rennthierjagd in Nordbritannien im 10—12. Jh. nachweist

cf. ibid. The compound is otherwise unattested, in Norse as well. The first element means 'reindeer'. Since the word is (h)rân in Old English but raine (rayne) in Norse, it is presumably a loanword, again designating a particular breed of dog. Reindeer bones in Caithness and Sutherland are known to Bugge, Helge Digtare in .. Edda, and to MAURER, who in Engl. Stud. 1895, p. 61, demonstrates reindeer hunting in northern Britain in the 10th–12th centuries
